facts.text: Symsonia was originally called Slabtown in the 1820s because sawmill slabs were used to lay roads and reduce mud.
The community’s name changed to Symsonia when a post office opened on December 23, 1847, with James K. Wilson as first postmaster.
In the mid‑19th century, the Wadesboro Road linked Calloway County to Paducah, spurring Symsonia’s growth as a farmers’ and lumbermen’s outpost.
The oldest surviving home in Symsonia, built in 1840, was constructed from bricks handmade by enslaved workers on site.
During the late 1930s, the Tennessee Valley Authority’s Kentucky Dam project hired Symsonia residents like Victor Jarvis, who earned $5.80 a day surveying and building the dam.
Because it sits between the East and West Forks of the Clarks River, Symsonia has faced recurrent flooding, prompting a 1975 federal disaster declaration.
